summary:
The United Arab Emirates subjects trans visitors to gender-document screening at the border. In 2025, two Israeli trans women were detained for hours at Dubai airport, X-rayed to check whether their genitals matched the female sex recorded in their passports, mocked by staff, and denied entry with their passports confiscated.

Entry refusals on identity grounds are documented across a decade. In August 2016 the trans media personality Gigi Gorgeous was denied entry and detained at Dubai airport. In March 2022 the Thai trans model Rachaya Noppakaroon, 2014 Miss Tiffany Universe runner-up, was stopped at Dubai immigration and interrogated for nine hours before being deported to Thailand ahead of her Expo 2020 appearance; her passport listed male sex while she lives as a woman.

The legal framework underpinning these encounters explicitly acknowledges and penalises nonconformity with traditional gender roles, and transgender expression or unconventional appearance frequently results in arrest, confinement or expulsion. A new federal criminal code enacted in early 2022 criminalised consensual same-sex relations with up to six months' imprisonment, and charges under it require a complaint basis.

There is no legal gender recognition in the UAE, so a visitor's documents cannot be brought into line with lived gender before travel. Foreign nationals also face prolonged custody: a Brazilian trans woman has been detained since September 2022, arrested after refusing a police-requested toxicology test, and in April 2023 she accused the consulate of negligence over her case.
tangentialFactors:
Article 409 of the 2022 federal criminal code reaches unmarried different-sex couples as well, indicating that the code's reach is not confined to same-sex conduct and that cohabitation status can itself become a legal exposure for visitors.

The requirement that charges rest on a complaint basis narrows the route to prosecution but does not narrow the border encounter: entry refusal, interrogation and deportation occur administratively, outside any complaint process, as the 2016, 2022 and 2025 airport cases show.

Outcomes for trans foreigners vary between refusal of entry, deportation and extended detention, and the record offers no basis for predicting which applies in a given case. Consular protection has proved weak in at least one documented instance, with a detainee publicly accusing her consulate of negligence.
localsOnly:
Legal gender recognition is unavailable to UAE residents, so residents cannot obtain official documents matching their gender, and the mismatch persists in every interaction with police, courts and employers.

LGBTI organisations cannot register in the UAE, leaving residents with no formal association through which to document arrests or press for protection.

The federal criminal code's six-month maximum for consensual same-sex relations applies to residents alongside visitors, and the gender-nonconformity provisions described by Cairo 52 operate through arrest, confinement and expulsion powers that fall most heavily on those living in the country.
outOfScopeNotes:
Whether genital X-ray screening at Dubai airport is a written procedure or an ad hoc practice by individual officers is not resolved by the available sources; the 2025 account establishes that it occurred, not that it is codified.

No source in the inventory gives conviction or sentencing data under the 2022 code's six-month provision, so the frequency of enforcement is unresolved.

The inventory does not address hate-crime protection, healthcare access, bathroom or facilities rules, or partner recognition for trans visitors; nothing should be inferred about those from the entries above.

Cairo 52 describes legal mechanisms penalising gender nonconformity without naming the specific articles relied on, so the statutory basis of those provisions remains unresolved here.

The outcome of the Brazilian detainee's case, and whether her consulate responded to the negligence allegation, are unresolved.
